title: Rate limiting, explained with a coffee shop

sections.text: Ever hit an API and got back a four twenty-nine: Too Many Requests? That's not a bug. Someone is guarding the door.

Picture a tiny coffee shop. On the counter sits a jar of tickets, and every customer has to take one before they can order. Once every second, the barista drops a fresh ticket into the jar. It only holds six, so when it's full, extra tickets simply fall away. Now a crowd rushes in. The first six grab tickets and get served right away. Everyone after that waits for the next ticket to drop.
That's a token bucket, the classic way servers do rate limiting. The jar is the bucket, the tickets are tokens, and each customer is a request.
Each request spends one token. When a request arrives and the bucket is empty, the server answers four twenty-nine, and can tell the client when to try again.
You've seen this in the wild. GitHub's API gives a signed-in user five thousand requests an hour, and every response tells you how many are left.
Here's the part pros tune. The bucket size decides how big a burst you allow. The refill rate decides your average. Set both, and one noisy client can't flood your API for everyone else.
So: refill at a steady rate, spend one token per request, and say no politely when it's empty.

analogy.setting: a small coffee shop with a ticket jar on the counter

mapping.everyday: barista adding a ticket each second

real_example: GitHub REST API primary rate limit for authenticated users (5,000 requests/hour) and its x-ratelimit-limit / x-ratelimit-remaining response headers.
claims: HTTP status 429 means Too Many Requests.
A 429 response can include a Retry-After header telling the client when to retry.
GitHub's REST API allows 5,000 requests per hour for authenticated users.
GitHub API responses include x-ratelimit-limit and x-ratelimit-remaining headers.
In a token bucket, capacity bounds the burst size and the refill rate bounds the long-run average rate.
